# AI Agents in Game Development: FOMO, Real Production Lessons, Failed Experiments, and AI Workshop Plan

--

## What it is all about

Every few days, it feels like the whole software industry has already moved to another planet.

Someone on Twitter/X has a small army of agents running 24/7. Someone else built a game from one prompt. Another post shows a 10 Mac mini coding setup where the human looks almost optional.

And then you go back to your actual game project, open the bug tracker, look at the build, read the playtest feedback, and think:

Are we the only ones still stuck in this reality, not knowing how to use that new AI stuff with million of likes on Twitter/X for the tasks we’re working on? Or maybe we’re just too slow, unskilled, or lazy, and the whole world is simply ahead of us?

This article is our honest attempt to answer that question, so developers who feel the same way can worry less and get back to what they love: building great things for everyone.

P.S. In the article, I use the word “LLM,” but my colleague told me it’s too nerdy and that I should call it AI, AI Agents, or at least Claude or Codex. I will do my best.

## Our “Reality”

We are Luden.io , a game studio making indie and educational games, including SuperWEIRD . We use LLM (oh, I mean AI ofcourse) tools every day: for code, design documents, QA, automation, translations, research, text editing, and prototyping.

But we do not use them in the way the internet sometimes makes it look. We use it in narrow areas of development in a fairly boring way.

To clarify further — in most tasks, we don’t use LLMs (I mean AI Agents) because we’ve already spent a few weekends in the office trying to roll out hotfixes after using LLMs, even in a very careful way.

And we still spend a lot of time doing normal, messy, human game development work.

## Our Tech Stack

- Defold Game Engine (3 projects)

- Unity (2 projects)

- Cursor (5 developers)

- VS Code (2 developers)

- Codex (6 developers)

- Antigravity (2 developers)

- Claude Code (1 developer) — and the same person is using Defold Script Editor instead of any IDE since he is a big fan

- Cloudflare and a bunch on VPS for network infrastructure on servers.com

- GitHub Repositories, GitHub Issues, GitHub Actions (running all our builds and automations on two mac mini in the office)

- Google Spreadsheets, Google Docs, Figma, NextCloud

### 1/7 Optimization

Sometimes we know exactly where the game is slow: performance drops in a specific scene, CPU/GPU time spikes in a specific system, a loop allocates too much memory.

In these cases, we can point the model at a large code area, explain what part of the game it belongs to, and ask for performance ideas. Sometimes it suggests a useful fix. More often, it finds strange inefficient code we missed. Not genius code. Usually, silly code like searching by string where a hash would be enough, or redrawing every frame things that shouldn’t be redrawn.

We tried to build a loop where an AI agent reads the game’s performance profiler data, makes changes, runs the game, and then reads the profiler data again.

It was very fun to build, but we did not find anything useful with this approach.

We also optimizing meshes for 2D sprites. We showed the agent the kind of mesh we wanted, then let it process several hundred sprites.

### 2/7 Bug fixes

A player sends a save file, stack trace, error report, or all of them together. We ask an AI agent to review the files along with the source code to help narrow down the possible causes and suggest a fix. This can work extremely well, especially in prototypes and internal tools built around state transitions, replays, or Redux-like architecture .

During the iterations, we found that text representations of the game state, logs, and replays are very helpful.

The most game-changing thing here is any state management architecture that lets you inspect the current world state and its changes in a text format. Even better if it’s deterministic. Here is an example of the architecture we are relying on.

Also — the better the text-based representation our engine provides, the better the results of this step will be. Defold is excellent here because it now offers a localhost web interface, so agents can do almost everything with the game and get scene data, profiler output, runtime logs, build logs, and many other things in text format.

### 3/7 Suggesting QA scenarios

QA engineer asks an AI agent to review the last milestone’s changes in GitHub and propose unusual testing scenarios where players might encounter bugs.

Weird combinations of new and old systems often break the game, but these scenarios are not always obvious.

But some catch exactly the kind of edge case that is easy to forget when everyone is tired.

### 4/7 Game design doc review like it’s code review

We store design documents in Markdown, close to the project. Over the years, we learned what design mistakes we tend to make as a studio:

Overcomplicated systems proposed with the idea that we would explain them to players “ somehow ” later. Too much information on one screen. Several conceptual steps hidden inside a single UI moment. And more.

So we wrote down our design principles and common mistakes.

Then we built a review process around them.

If programmers can review code changes before merging them, why can’t we review design document changes in the same way?

When a designer changes a document, an agent reviews the diff, checks it against our rules, raises questions, and suggests possible fixes.

It does not always find the right issue, but it sometimes catches real problems before they become implemented problems.

Wait, but how do you keep all the design documentation up to date? That should take an enormous amount of time, right?

That’s correct. The answer here is Codex voice input. Since we ask the agent to make changes in the Markdown files, it’s like giving the agent a coding task. So after a game design meeting, we give it a voice follow-up and then check whether it updated the design docs correctly.

We use Codex Cloud and the ChatGPT iOS app for that. Codex checks out the game design documentation repository on a cloud server, makes changes we asked for using voice input, creates a pull request, and does the code review — I mean, the doc review — while we’re walking back to our computers from a meeting room in the office.

⚠️ Warning for bigger projects!

As the project grows, it becomes very useful to split the documentation into a core game design document and separate additions, such as major update scopes or subsystem/submodule docs.

When we tried to keep everything in one large document, the autoreview process kept asking us to explain many details that were obvious to the developers but not to the LLM. It assumed those details were missing not because they were obvious, but because we did not plan to implement them, which made the game seem worse.

### 5/7 Automations, prototypes, isolated modules

One of the best, most practical uses for agents is handling small parts of everyday work. To automate tasks or build something isolated, you usually only need simple solutions.

For example:

- Create a GitHub Action or messenger bot to clean up GitHub issues, build games, run tests, and upload game builds to platforms

- Translate and check techincal tags in the in-game texts (By the way, we got much better translation quality when we started providing the same text in two languages as input — for example, English and Greek)

- Format Steam posts

- Build a Cloudflare Worker

- Add Twitch API integration for a game (with Twitch docs provided and Codex plan mode)

- Convert platforms’ sales reports from “unique” format into Google Sheets

- Build a quick game prototype

These tasks do not require perfect architecture, high performance, deep understanding of the system— only a working result.

### 6/7 Updating static websites

Because we make educational video games, we have several websites that serve as step-by-step guides for educators and parents. For example, edu.superweird.io . They explain how to play the games with children and how to set up class activities for small groups or individual students. These websites are also where users play the games, since many of them use Chromebooks and access our games through the browser.

Whenever we receive feedback about what felt unintuitive or where users were unsure what to do, we can usually improve the guides by feeding that feedback into an AI agent, which then helps improve both the guides and the website itself.

The websites are hosted on Cloudflare Pages.

### 7/7 Analytics for social media content and in-game stats

After publishing content on TikTok , YouTube Shorts , or Instagram Reels, and after running small Reddit or Twitter ad campaigns, we send all performance data to an LLM to get insights and actionable recommendations for improvement. Most of them are about the timing of the video’s boring moments.

If we also have the video script with timestamps, which we usually do, the analysis becomes much more accurate. This helps identify what was happening on screen at the exact moment when many viewers stopped watching.

We do the same with Amplitude analytics for in-game events. In most cases, the main use case is asking Amplitude to build a specific graph or funnel.

## What doesn’t work

For each block in this section, it’s fair to say: you just did it the wrong way, with not detailed enough plan, the project’s architecture is not modular/testable enough, used the wrong model, and the wrong harness — that’s why it doesn’t work. The answer to this is in the “LLM Week” section later in the article.

### Implementing gameplay features

We tried to get agents to plan, implement, test, and polish entire gameplay features.

In theory, this sounds perfect. In practice, it is fragile because there are an enormous number of details the agent can get wrong, even though they are usually quite straightforward for a game developer with general knowledge of video games.

Even with a large, detailed plan, answers to the model’s questions, extra techniques to improve the plan like grill-me, and sometimes another agent criticizing it, we still do not know whether the final implementation will be good or whether some important context will be lost.

A programmer implementing a game feature makes many small design decisions while writing code.

Even if that programmer is not the game designer, they understand the intended experience, the game’s systems, and the dangerous shortcuts.

An extremely detailed plan could probably help, but it is fair to say it takes longer and gives less certain results than manual implementation. By “manual,” I of course mean using modern IDEs with very smart autocomplete.

It should be said that system design and code architecture are the most important factors here, because it’s all about deciding where code should live and where the boundaries of each module should be. The clearer these boundaries are, the better the project scales with LLMs (I mean AI agents).
